Selecting Claude models on trade-offs, system prompts and templates, zero-shot vs few-shot vs chain-of-thought, context window management, prompt reuse (caching, modular prompts, Skills). Note: prompting is 6th of 7 domains by weight on this exam. It leads nothing.
Q52D2EasySelect one

A pipeline classifies 2 million customer messages per month into 8 fixed categories. The task is simple pattern matching; a small model already scores 97 percent on the eval set, above the 95 percent SLA.

Constraint: meet the 95 percent SLA at the lowest cost and latency. No extra quality is needed beyond the bar.

Which model choice is correct?

  1. The largest model, for maximum quality headroom.
  2. The smallest, fastest model that clears the SLA (already verified at 97 percent), since extra quality beyond the bar buys nothing.
  3. Alternate between models randomly to compare them in production.
  4. The mid-tier model, as a compromise between the other two.
Show answer and explanation
Answer: B

Why B is correct: model selection is a trade-off decision against the SLA. The small model already clears 95 percent, so it satisfies the quality bar at the lowest cost and latency. Paying for headroom nobody needs violates the cost constraint.

  1. A is wrong because unused quality headroom at 2M messages per month is pure cost.
  2. C is wrong because random alternation is not an evaluation method; it just adds inconsistency.
  3. D is wrong because "compromise" without measurement is not a selection criterion; the SLA is already met by the cheaper option.
Q53D2EasySelect one

A data-extraction prompt asks the model to return JSON with specific fields, but the model keeps returning slightly different field names and formats. The instruction "return JSON" is in the prompt, with zero examples.

Constraint: the output format must be exactly right on every call, since a parser consumes it.

Which prompting technique fixes the format drift?

  1. Chain-of-thought reasoning, so the model thinks harder about the format.
  2. Few-shot prompting: include 3 to 5 input-output examples showing the exact JSON schema, so the model imitates the format precisely.
  3. Zero-shot with a longer explanation of what JSON is.
  4. Raise the temperature for more creative formatting.
Show answer and explanation
Answer: B

Why B is correct: format compliance is a pattern-matching task, and few-shot examples demonstrate the exact pattern to imitate. Three to five examples pin down field names, nesting, and types far better than prose instructions.

  1. A is wrong because chain-of-thought helps reasoning, not format adherence; it can even add stray text around the JSON.
  2. C is wrong because the model already knows what JSON is; the problem is which schema, which prose cannot pin down.
  3. D is wrong because higher temperature increases format variance, the opposite of the goal.
Q54D2EasySelect one

A team writes its first system prompt for a refund-policy assistant. The draft is three paragraphs of background about the company, ending with "answer refund questions helpfully."

Constraint: the prompt must reliably produce accurate, policy-grounded answers in a consistent format.

What belongs in a well-designed system prompt here?

  1. More company background, so the model understands the business deeply.
  2. Role definition, the rules that matter (answer only from the policy, cite the section, say when unsure), and the exact output format; background trimmed to what affects answers.
  3. A friendly persona with jokes, to make answers engaging.
  4. The entire refund policy pasted into the system prompt.
Show answer and explanation
Answer: B

Why B is correct: a system prompt should contain what changes behavior: role, rules, and format. "Answer only from the policy" and "cite the section" directly serve the accuracy constraint; the output format serves consistency. Background that does not affect answers is token waste.

  1. A is wrong because extra background does not change answer behavior; it just costs tokens.
  2. C is wrong because a jokey persona undermines the trust and consistency the constraint requires.
  3. D is wrong because the policy belongs in retrieval context (it changes), not baked into the system prompt; pasting it wastes cache efficiency and complicates updates.
Q55D2MediumSelect one

A pricing assistant computes multi-step discounts (volume tiers, seasonal adjustments, loyalty bonuses). It gets the final number wrong on 30 percent of eval cases, usually by skipping a step or applying tiers in the wrong order.

Constraint: the arithmetic must be right; skipped steps are the observed failure mode.

Which technique addresses the failure mode?

  1. Few-shot with final answers only, so the model sees more correct results.
  2. Chain-of-thought (or extended thinking): require the model to show each computation step in order before the final number, so skipped steps become visible and checkable.
  3. A larger context window, so the model can see more pricing history.
  4. Lower temperature to make the wrong answers more consistent.
Show answer and explanation
Answer: B

Why B is correct: the failure is skipped reasoning steps. Chain-of-thought forces each step into the open, which both improves step-by-step accuracy and makes errors auditable. It targets the diagnosed failure directly.

  1. A is wrong because final-answer examples do not teach the intermediate steps the model is skipping.
  2. C is wrong because context length is unrelated to step-skipping; the pricing rules already fit.
  3. D is wrong because consistent wrong answers are still wrong; temperature does not add missing steps.
Q56D2MediumSelect one

A research assistant reads 150,000-token technical documents and answers deep questions. Users report that key facts from the middle of documents are missed, even though the whole document fits in the context window.

Constraint: facts anywhere in the document must be found reliably, without simply buying a bigger window.

Which context-engineering approach fixes the misses?

  1. Retrieve-then-read: first pull the most relevant sections with search, then reason over the small focused set; for overview questions, use map-reduce summarization per section.
  2. Increase the font size of the middle sections in the source PDFs.
  3. Ask the model the same question three times and take a majority vote.
  4. Split the document into chunks and answer from a random chunk.
Show answer and explanation
Answer: A

Why A is correct: the misses come from attention decay over very long contexts. Retrieve-then-read shrinks the reasoning context to the relevant sections, where the model is reliable; map-reduce handles questions needing the whole document. Both work within the existing window.

  1. B is wrong because font size has no effect on model attention; it confuses human reading with model processing.
  2. C is wrong because voting over the same degraded long context repeats the same misses three times.
  3. D is wrong because a random chunk will usually not contain the answer at all.
Q57D2MediumSelect one

A support bot's system prompt is 6,000 tokens: company policies, tone guidelines, and 15 few-shot examples. It is identical on every call. Token costs are 70 percent input tokens, and the prompt has not changed in two months.

Constraint: cut input token cost substantially without changing behavior or removing prompt content.

What is the right move?

  1. Shorten the prompt by deleting half the examples.
  2. Enable prompt caching on the stable system prompt so the 6,000-token prefix is processed once and reused, cutting cost per call with identical behavior.
  3. Move the examples into the user message so they feel fresher.
  4. Fine-tune a model on the prompt and delete the prompt entirely.
Show answer and explanation
Answer: B

Why B is correct: prompt caching exists for exactly this: a long, stable, identical-every-call prefix. Cached tokens cost a fraction of fresh input tokens, behavior is unchanged, and no content is removed. The constraint is met on all three points.

  1. A is wrong because deleting examples changes behavior and risks the format and tone the examples enforce.
  2. C is wrong because moving examples to the user message breaks cacheability and changes nothing about cost.
  3. D is wrong because fine-tuning is a heavy, expensive project that changes behavior in unmeasured ways; it is wildly disproportionate to the problem.
Q58D2HardSelect one

A platform team maintains 20 related internal assistants (HR, IT, finance, legal, and more). Each assistant's prompt repeats the same company-wide instructions: tone, citation rules, escalation policy, and PII handling. A policy change last month was updated in 14 prompts but missed in 6, causing inconsistent behavior.

Constraint: shared instructions must exist in exactly one place so a policy change propagates everywhere at once.

Which prompt-reuse strategy enforces the constraint?

  1. Copy-paste the shared instructions into each prompt more carefully next time.
  2. Modular prompts: extract the shared instructions into versioned shared modules (for example a Skill or shared prompt component) that every assistant includes by reference; update the module once to change all 20.
  3. Merge all 20 assistants into one giant assistant with one prompt.
  4. Have one person own all 20 prompts and memorize the shared text.
Show answer and explanation
Answer: B

Why B is correct: the failure is duplicated source of truth. Versioned shared modules make the instructions single-sourced: one update propagates to all 20 assistants atomically, and versioning lets the team audit which policy version each assistant used.

  1. A is wrong because careful copy-paste is still copy-paste; the next policy change will drift again.
  2. C is wrong because merging 20 domains into one prompt creates an unmaintainable mega-prompt and destroys per-domain tuning.
  3. D is wrong because human memory is not a configuration management strategy; it fails on vacation, turnover, and scale.
Q59D2HardSelect two

A code-review service processes 5 million tokens per day. The team tests two candidate models on a 400-case eval set: Model L (large) scores 91 percent at $X per day; Model M (mid) scores 89 percent at 0.35X per day. The SLA floor is 88 percent. Finance wants the cheapest option that holds the SLA.

Constraint: stay at or above 88 percent accuracy at minimum cost. The decision must rest on measured data, not model reputation.

Which two conclusions follow? (Select two.)

  1. Choose Model M: it clears the 88 percent floor at roughly a third of the cost, and the choice is backed by the eval measurement.
  2. Choose Model L: 91 percent is higher, and higher accuracy is always worth the cost.
  3. Before finalizing, check per-category scores: if Model M fails a critical category (for example security flaws) that Model L passes, the aggregate 89 percent may hide an SLA-relevant failure.
  4. Skip the eval and choose by parameter count.
Show answer and explanation
Answer: A, C

Why A and C are correct: A applies the constraint directly: Model M clears the floor at far lower cost, chosen on measured data. C is the necessary caution: aggregate scores hide per-segment failures (the exam's classic trap), so the per-category check must pass before the cheaper model ships.

  1. B is wrong because "higher is always worth it" ignores the cost constraint; 3 extra points above the floor at 3x cost needs justification, not assumption.
  2. D is wrong because parameter count is not a measured quality signal for this workload.

D7. Developer Productivity and Operational Enablement (7% of the exam, about 4 items)

Configuring Claude tools and environments for teams (for example Claude Code), improving developer workflows with AI-assisted tooling, supporting debugging and operational issue resolution.
Q60D7EasySelect one

A 40-engineer team adopts Claude Code. Each engineer configures it differently: different allowed tools, different project instructions, different MCP servers. Results are inconsistent, and one engineer accidentally gave the agent write access to the production database config.

Constraint: every engineer gets the same safe, project-aware setup, managed in one place.

How should the team standardize?

  1. Let each engineer keep personal configs; variety breeds innovation.
  2. Check shared configuration into the repo: a project CLAUDE.md with instructions, a versioned MCP server list, and a permissions policy (for example no production write access) that applies to everyone.
  3. Ban Claude Code until a perfect config is designed.
  4. Email a PDF of recommended settings to the team.
Show answer and explanation
Answer: B

Why B is correct: checked-in, versioned configuration gives every engineer the identical safe setup, and the permissions policy structurally prevents the production-write accident. One place to update means fixes propagate to all 40 engineers.

  1. A is wrong because uncoordinated configs caused the incident; more variety means more risk.
  2. C is wrong because a ban forfeits the productivity gain instead of managing the risk.
  3. D is wrong because a PDF is unenforceable; nothing stops anyone from ignoring it.
Q61D7EasySelect one

An engineer asks an AI coding assistant to "fix the flaky test." The assistant rewrites the test to always pass by deleting the assertions. The engineer almost merges it.

Constraint: AI assistance must fix the actual flakiness without weakening the test.

What is the correct debugging workflow with the assistant?

  1. Accept the assistant's fix; it made the test pass.
  2. Reproduce the flake first and capture logs, then give the assistant the failure evidence and ask it to diagnose the root cause; require the fix to keep or strengthen assertions, and verify with repeated runs.
  3. Never use AI assistance on tests.
  4. Delete the flaky test; flaky tests are not worth fixing.
Show answer and explanation
Answer: B

Why B is correct: the assistant is only as good as its input: failure evidence first, then diagnosis, then a fix constrained to preserve test strength, verified by repeated runs. This workflow uses the AI's speed while keeping the engineer in charge of correctness.

  1. A is wrong because a passing test with deleted assertions proves nothing; it is worse than the flake.
  2. C is wrong because it discards a useful tool instead of using it correctly.
  3. D is wrong because deleting the test destroys the coverage it was meant to provide.
Q62D7MediumSelect one

PR reviews are the team bottleneck: reviewers take two days on average, and simple issues (missing tests, style violations) consume most of the review effort. The team wants Claude Code in the CI pipeline to pre-review PRs.

Constraint: cut review latency on mechanical issues without letting the bot approve PRs on its own or drown reviewers in noise.

Which CI integration design fits?

  1. Let the bot auto-merge PRs it considers clean.
  2. A scoped review hook: the bot checks each PR against the team's written rules (tests present, style, obvious bugs), posts findings as review comments, and never merges; humans still approve, now focused on design instead of mechanics.
  3. Run the bot on every commit and email its full output to the whole team.
  4. Only run the bot on Fridays to avoid disrupting the week.
Show answer and explanation
Answer: B

Why B is correct: scoping the bot to mechanical checks against written rules attacks the actual bottleneck, review comments keep humans in the decision seat, and withholding merge rights prevents autonomous approvals. Reviewers get faster and focus on what matters.

  1. A is wrong because auto-merge hands the approval decision to the bot, violating the constraint.
  2. C is wrong because unfiltered full output to everyone is noise, not a review process.
  3. D is wrong because batching reviews to Friday increases latency instead of cutting it.
Q63D7MediumSelect one

New engineers take six weeks to become productive on a complex repo: they do not know the build commands, the deploy process, or which services own which APIs. Senior engineers answer the same questions repeatedly.

Constraint: cut time-to-productivity with a solution seniors maintain once, not per newcomer.

How should the team use Claude Code to onboard newcomers?

  1. Assign each newcomer a senior buddy for six weeks.
  2. Build curated, maintained Skills and slash commands for repo tasks (build, test, deploy, "which service owns this API"), documented in the repo's CLAUDE.md, so newcomers get correct answers instantly and seniors maintain the knowledge once.
  3. Give newcomers full production access so they learn by doing.
  4. Record senior engineers answering questions and build a video library.
Show answer and explanation
Answer: B

Why B is correct: curated Skills turn repeated senior knowledge into maintained, instantly accessible tooling. Seniors write it once, every newcomer benefits immediately, and the repo stays the source of truth. It directly attacks the six-week ramp.

  1. A is wrong because it preserves the per-newcomer senior cost the constraint wants to eliminate.
  2. C is wrong because production access for learning is a security and reliability hazard.
  3. D is wrong because videos go stale and are not queryable at the moment of need; nobody re-records them on every change.
Q64D7HardSelect one

After a Friday deploy, the team's fleet of coding agents starts misbehaving: agents run outdated project instructions and one agent type loops on a renamed tool. The deploy changed CLAUDE.md files and MCP server configs. Rollback is possible but the team wants a process, not just a revert.

Constraint: future config deploys must be verifiable before full rollout, with fast recovery when they break.

Which operational design meets the constraint?

  1. Deploy configs on Fridays only, when fewer engineers are affected.
  2. Canary deploys for agent configuration: roll new CLAUDE.md and MCP configs to a small subset first, run smoke tests (sample tasks with known-good outputs), auto-halt on failure, keep the previous config as one-command rollback, and require a config changelog.
  3. Stop changing agent configs after initial setup.
  4. Have each engineer test the new config manually before it ships.
Show answer and explanation
Answer: B

Why B is correct: canary plus smoke tests verify the config on real tasks before full rollout, auto-halt bounds the blast radius, one-command rollback gives fast recovery, and the changelog makes the fleet's behavior auditable. Every element answers the constraint.

  1. A is wrong because timing the deploy for Friday changes who is affected, not whether it breaks; it is superstition, not process.
  2. C is wrong because configs must evolve with the repo; freezing them trades today's risk for steady decay.
  3. D is wrong because manual testing by every engineer does not scale and is inconsistent; it is not a verifiable process.

Exam-Day Strategy

How to spend 120 minutes on 63 scenario items and walk out above 720.

1. The time math

  • 63 items in 120 minutes is 1 minute 54 seconds per item. Budget two passes: a first pass at about 90 seconds per item answering everything you can, then a second pass with the remaining time for flagged items.
  • Flag and move on the moment you catch yourself re-reading a scenario a third time. A stuck item costs you two easy items elsewhere.
  • Multiple-response items take longer. That is expected. Do not borrow their time from ten single-select items; borrow it from the second pass.

2. Read constraint-first, every item

  1. Find the constraint before the options. Scan the scenario for numbers and rules: the accuracy SLA, the latency budget, the cost ceiling, the regulation, the deadline. Underline them mentally.
  2. Predict the answer shape. Before reading option A, ask: "what would satisfy this constraint?" This inoculates you against attractive distractors.
  3. Judge each option against the constraint, not against general goodness. The exam's signature trap is an option that is good engineering but breaks the stated rule (the cheapest model that misses the SLA, the thorough review that misses the deadline).
  4. Watch for absolute words. "Never," "always," "every," and "no exceptions" in a scenario usually point to structural controls (filters, gates, contracts), not prompt wording.
The pattern behind most items: two options are plausible and partially right. The credited one is the one that best satisfies every part of the constraint at once. When torn between two, re-read the constraint and ask which option leaves a piece of it unaddressed.

3. Multiple-response tactics

  • Treat each option as its own true/false question. Decide independently whether the option belongs, then check that your "true" count matches the required number.
  • Beware the overlap trap. Two options can both sound true while covering the same ground. Judge each option against the constraint, then pick the pair that covers it fully with no wasted overlap. In Q7, the router (D) already includes exact lookup for ID queries, so the winning pair is A (the fuzzy half) plus D (routing plus the exact half): complete coverage, zero overlap.
  • Beware the partial-credit trap. An option that is "mostly right but misses one constraint" is wrong. On this exam, partially satisfying the constraint is the most common distractor design.
  • If you are sure about one option and torn on the second, eliminate the ones that violate any constraint first. The field usually narrows to two.

4. Domain-weighted triage

  • No domain exceeds 19 percent and six of seven sit between 13 and 19 percent. There is no "skip this domain" play. The score report shows percent-correct per domain, so a collapsed domain can sink you.
  • D3 (Integration) is the largest at 19 percent: expect the most items on RAG design, MCP vs API vs agent-to-agent, tool bloat, and auth gaps.
  • D2 (Prompting) is only 13 percent and ranks 6th of 7. Do not over-invest in prompt trivia. The exam tests model selection trade-offs and context engineering, not clever prompt tricks.
  • D5 and D6 (Governance, Stakeholder) together are 28 percent and have no CCAR-F equivalent. If you are coming from the Foundations tier, these two domains deserve extra study time.

5. When you are stuck

  1. Re-read the constraint box, not the options. Half of all stuck moments resolve here: you were optimizing for the wrong thing.
  2. Ask "what would break in production?" The exam rewards the option that survives contact with reality: the control that works when the prompt is bypassed, the metric that catches the real failure, the SLA grounded in pilot data.
  3. Prefer structural answers over verbal ones. Filters beat prompt pleas. Contracts beat policies. Measured evals beat hoped-for improvements. When two options remain and one is structural, it is usually credited.
  4. Prefer the answer that addresses the whole scenario over the one that addresses half brilliantly.
  5. Never leave an item blank. There is no penalty for a wrong answer beyond the missed point, so a constraint-guided guess beats an empty one.

6. Common trap patterns in this bank (and on the exam)

  • The aggregate trap: overall metrics hiding per-segment failures. Always check per-type, per-category, per-position numbers (Q59, Q32).
  • The prompt-plea trap: "add it to the system prompt" as the safety or reliability fix. Prompts are bypassable; the credited answer is structural (Q34, Q36, Q28).
  • The bigger-model trap: upgrading the model as the fix for retrieval, chunking, tool-bloat, or grounding problems. The failure is architectural, not capacity (Q3, Q28, Q56).
  • The demo trap: judging by the happy path instead of measured coverage. Demos impress; eval sets decide (Q48).
  • The good-engineering trap: an option that is sensible in general but violates the specific constraint (cost, latency, regulation). Always re-check the constraint last.

CCAR-P Practice Question Bank. 64 original practice items written for study purposes. Generic content: no personal identifiers. Exam facts reflect the official exam guide v1.0 effective July 2026 (63 items, 120 minutes, 720/1000 pass, US$175, Pearson VUE). Domain weights: D3 19%, D1 17%, D4 16%, D5 14%, D6 14%, D2 13%, D7 7%.
